after.authors: Kittrell, H. D.; Kauffman, J.; Smit, R. A. J.; Atabaki, N. N.; Merino, J.; Walker, R. W.; Loos, R. J. F.; Nadkarni, G. N.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
after.abstract: Introduction. Diet quality scores are well-established predictors of cardiometabolic health but compress an individuals food intake into a single dimension, potentially masking dietary variation relevant to disease risk. Whether this hidden variation carries prognostic information has not been tested at scale. Methods. We applied non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) to the reported intake of 148 individual foods and beverages from 87,162 UK Biobank participants. We tested the association of NMF-derived intake factors with incident coronary artery disease (CAD), type 2 diabetes (T2D) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) over a median 9.4 years of follow-up using Cox proportional hazards models. We evaluated the prognostic value of the factors beyond diet quality scores using stepwise Cox models and net reclassification improvement (NRI), and characterized their metabolic profiles through metabolome-wide association analyses (MWAS) of 249 circulating metabolites. Results. NMF identified eight reproducible intake factors that were stable across geographically distinct samples. Four factors were significantly associated with incident cardiometabolic disease: a high sugar and processed foods factor was adversely associated with T2D (HR 1.19; 95% CI 1.11-1.27) and CKD (HR 1.15; 1.07-1.23), while a plant-based and fish factor was protective for CKD (HR 0.90; 0.84-0.96) and a cheese and whole grains factor was protective for CAD (HR 0.94; 0.90-0.98). The factors improved disease discrimination beyond both diet quality scores ( {Delta}C up to +0.0049) and correctly reclassified 8-16% more individuals, whereas adding either score to models containing the factors produced negligible further improvement. The high sugar and processed foods factor was associated with depletion of omega-3 fatty acids and the plant-based and fish factor showed enrichment in polyunsaturated fatty acids. Conclusions. Food-level dietary intake profiling captures clinically relevant variation that established diet quality scores mask, offering a path toward more personalized dietary assessment for cardiometabolic disease prevention.

after.authors: Shi, Y.; Niarchou, M.; Zhang, Y.; Lee, Y. H.; Choi, K. W.; Blostein, F.; Straub, P.; Ge, T.; Feng, Y.-C. A.; Roth Mota, N.; Sprooten, E.; Franke, B.; Davis, L. K.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Radboud University Medical Center, Department of Human Genetics, Nijmegen, The Netherlands
after.abstract: Summary Background Current psychiatric diagnoses lack biological grounding. Using transdiagnostic psychiatric dimensions derived through data-driven genetic studies with large-scale clinical health records of multiple physiological and clinical outcomes, we can gain new insights into biological similarity and differences between such dimensions, informing nosological discourse. Methods Here, we examined data from 108,182 individuals of European-like ancestry and 13,229 African-like ancestry across two healthcare biobanks. Genetic liabilities of individuals were estimated as polygenic scores for five first-order psychopathology factors (compulsive, thought, neurodevelopmental, substance use, internalizing disorders) and one second-order factor (hierarchical/p-factor). Phenome-wide and laboratory-wide association scans encompassed 1,520 medical phenotypes and 123 laboratory metrics, meta-analyzed across sites. People with lived experience were involved in the design, preparation, interpretation and reporting of this work. Outcomes We observed robust associations with up to 143 conditions (14 disease categories) for first-order factors and 221 conditions (15 categories) for the hierarchical factor (OR=0.75-1.94). Circulatory, digestive, and respiratory diseases were linked to neurodevelopmental, internalizing, and substance use liabilities. Metabolic conditions were negatively associated with thought and compulsive liabilities but positively associated with the remaining three factors. Laboratory results, particularly lipid and glucose metabolism markers, supported these differential findings. Immune markers also showed differential associations, with C-reactive protein and Complement C4 specifically linked to neurodevelopmental and thought factors, respectively. Similar trends emerged in the smaller African-like ancestry sample. Interpretation Overall, these findings support ongoing efforts to define biologically informed subtypes in psychiatry, such as immuno-metabolic profiles, which can facilitate patient stratification in clinical trials and support transdiagnostic precision psychiatry approaches. Funding The work was supported by funding from the participating institutions. BF's and NRM's contributions were supported by the European Community's Horizon 2020 Programme (H2020/2014-2020) under grant agreement No. 847879 (PRIME). NRM was also supported by the Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research (NWO) Innovation Programme (Vidi grant No. 09150172410043). Research reported in this publication was also supported by the National Institute of Mental Health of the National Institutes of Health under Award Number R01MH124851. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the funders.

after.title: Preprint: Genetic architecture and polygenic prediction of self-reported response to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors in individuals with depression: a genome-wide meta-analysis
after.authors: Kamp, M.; Singh, M.; Hu, K.; Lo, C. W. H.; Watson, C. J.; Mitchell, B. L.; Thomas, J. T.; Breen, G.; Coleman, J. R.; Lee, S.-H.; Pain, O.; 23andMe Research Institute,  ; AMBER Research Team,  ; AGDS Research Team,  ; GLAD Study Consortium,  ; NIHR BioResource,  ; Lewis, C. M.
after.abstract: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are first-line treatments for depression, but response is highly variable, and no robust genetic predictors have been identified. We conducted a genome-wide association meta-analysis of self-reported SSRI response in 62,879 individuals of European ancestry with depression (72.6% responders) across six cohorts (seven datasets), followed by gene-set, transcriptomic, proteomic, drug-target and polygenic score (PGS) analyses. SNP-based heritability was modest but significant (h2 = 3.1%, SE = 1.4%) with no genome-wide significant variants detected. Gene-set analyses implicated gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission, and a gene involved in glutamate transport (SLC17A6) showed consistent sub-threshold evidence across pathway, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses. Drug-target enrichment for hypnotics, anxiolytics and general anesthetics further supported the GABAergic signal. A leave-one-out PGS from the discovery meta-analysis was associated with self-reported SSRI response in independent cohorts (meta-analysis OR = 1.05, 95% CI 1.02--1.08, p = 0.002). Higher PGS for depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), autism, addiction and schizophrenia were associated with lower odds of reported SSRI response, with ADHD, PTSD, autism and addiction remaining after adjustment for depression PGS. In contrast, educational attainment PGS was associated with better SSRI response. Self-reported SSRI response captures genetic insights relevant to antidepressant response, implicating GABAergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission. Individuals with higher genetic loading for psychiatric conditions report poorer response, and higher genetic loading for educational attainment PGS a better reported response. Although larger studies are needed to identify specific variants, self-report offers a practical, patient-centered and scalable route to collect the larger samples required.

after.title: Preprint: Automating postmarketing pharmacovigilance with large language model agents
after.authors: Zhang, R.; Zhou, Y.; Chui, C. S. L.; Yu, D.; Wu, Z.; Luo, R.
after.abstract: Postmarketing pharmacovigilance relies on spontaneous adverse event reporting and labor-intensive observational studies, which suffer from underreporting and delayed risk detection. Large language model (LLM) agents could automate real-world evidence generation, but generalist agents make ad hoc analytical decisions that compromise epidemiological validity and reproducibility. Here we present MedCheckpoint, a multi-agent LLM system for automated postmarketing pharmacovigilance. MedCheckpoint grounds each analytical stage in a curated, source-traceable medical knowledge base, locks core study-design parameters before execution, performs patient-level analyses with human-written deterministic statistical tools, and enforces checkpoint rules that abort infeasible analyses, with optional human-in-the-loop review. We evaluated MedCheckpoint using a 54-question benchmark on a dual-purpose simulated electronic health record (EHR) testbed of 2.7 million individuals, designed with reliable clinical signals to evaluate routine analytical accuracy alongside spurious signals to stress-test system rigor. Across the benchmark, MedCheckpoint outperformed two coding-agent baselines in report quality across five dimensions rated by three independent LLM judges (overall means 4.81-4.88 versus 4.25-4.55 and 4.02-4.29) and yielded higher run-to-run consistency (mean within-question standard deviation 0.116-0.186 versus up to 0.440). Crucially, while baselines failed on up to 2 of 21 runs when handling infeasible comparisons or unmeasurable outcomes, MedCheckpoint produced no misleading failures across all seven stress-test trap questions with known data limitations. MedCheckpoint enables reliable, auditable, and scalable pharmacovigilance analysis.

after.title: Preprint: An agent-based model of Epstein-Barr virus transmission and vaccination
after.authors: Amoako, B.; Huang, Z.; Thommes, E. W.; Hare, W.; Cojocaru, M. G.
after.abstract: Epstein- Barr virus (EBV) infects over 90\% of adults worldwide, causing infectious mononucleosis (IM) in adolescents and young adults and contributing to multiple malignancies. Despite its global burden, population- level transmission modeling of EBV remains limited. We present the first population- level agent-based model (ABM) of EBV transmission. The model is implemented with 10,000 agents and calibrated to age-specific seroprevalence data from the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Two complementary calibration methods are evaluated, each with its own distinct advantages: Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) and Bayesian Optimization with Expected Quantile Improvement (BO- EQI). ABC directly yields an approximate distribution of transmission parameters for propagation through vaccination scenarios. BO- EQI uses a limited simulation budget to identify well-fitting parameter vectors, particularly as the number of fitted parameters increases. We estimate parameter uncertainty at each resolution in a separate Gaussian-kernel posterior analysis, which requires additional simulations and an explicit model for discrepancies between simulated and observed prevalence. As an illustrative application, we simulate the population-level effect of hypothetical EBV vaccines over a 100-year projection horizon. Similar to a previous modeling study, our results suggest that vaccine durability is at least as critical as efficacy, and that a vaccine with direct protection against only EBV may persistently shift IM burden to older ages, an effect our longer simulation horizon reveals to be a durable equilibrium shift rather than a transient cohort phenomenon. These findings highlight the importance of careful vaccine target product profile design; in particular, our results suggest that dual efficacy against both EBV infection and IM progression represents the most promising achievable target profile, and should be a core design objective for next-generation EBV vaccines.

after.authors: Mayer-Blackwell, K.; Hussain, K.; Ebrahimi, N.; Ford, E. S.; Dale, A. P.; Alderson, J.; Bibi, S.; Munro, A. P. S.; Faust, S. N.; Liu, X.; Lambe, T.; Voysey, M.; Fiore-Gartland, A.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Vaccine and Infectious Disease Division, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, Seattle, USA; Vaccine Immunology Statistical Center, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, Seat
after.abstract: HLA-driven heterogeneity and limitations of live T cell functional assays routinely thwart assessment of cell-mediated immunity in vaccination trials. To address this, we developed a T-cell receptor (TCR)-based measure of immunogen recognition and evaluated it in COV-BOOST, a third-dose COVID-19 vaccine trial, during the Delta and Omicron waves (2021-2022, United Kingdom). We estimated HLA-aware Spike-reactive T cell (HA-TS) breadth from participant HLA genotypes, TCR{beta} repertoires, and a novel SARS-CoV-2 S HLA-linked reference catalog. Higher post-boost HA-TS breadth was associated with lower symptomatic infection risk (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.39-0.86). This association persisted after adjustment for neutralizing antibody titers and IFN-{gamma} responses. Examination of HA-TS across prior studies showed that it reflects participant genotype, exposure intensity, and time from exposure to sampling. These findings highlight the possibility that estimates of antigen-specific T cell repertoire breadth could serve as a correlate of protection to accelerate vaccine development.

after.title: Preprint: Phylogeography and transmission dynamics of the 2025-2026 Utah-Arizona measles outbreak: a retrospective genomic epidemiology study
after.authors: Marye, A.; Oakeson, K.; Lan, Y.; Warren, J. L.; Francis, D.; Hicks, L.; Walter, K.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Utah Department of Health and Human Services
after.abstract: Background: Measles outbreaks are increasing in frequency globally as vaccine coverage decreases. During the 2025-26 Utah-Arizona border outbreak, identifying where and between whom transmission occurred was essential for directing control measures. However, epidemiological data alone are not sufficient to infer transmission patterns. Methods: As part of the local and state-wide outbreak investigation, we conducted amplicon-based whole genome sequencing on residual diagnostic samples from confirmed measles cases collected from June 15, 2025-April 30, 2026. We reconstructed viral dispersal across Utah using Bayesian phylogeographic analyses. We evaluated genetic distance thresholds for identifying recent transmission by comparing single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based genetic clusters with known epidemiologic linkages. We then assessed pairwise exposures associated with genetically supported transmission linkage using logistic regression, accounting for network and spatial dependence between pairs. Findings: We generated 509 high-quality whole measles virus genomes from 913 patients. In 2025, most viral dispersal events (67.9%) originated in Southwest Utah and Mohave County, Arizona, where the first cases were reported. By 2026, most viral spread (60.5%) occurred outside of this area. A threshold of 0 SNPs identified epidemiologically linked pairs of individuals with a sensitivity of 77.4% and specificity of 92.3%. Household membership (odds ratio (OR): 219.10, 95% credible interval (CI): 112.66-325.53), participation in the same sport (OR: 15.19, 95% CI: 9.75-20.63), and attendance at the same school (OR: 51.5, 95% CI: 36.38-66.61) were independently associated with transmission linkage. Increasing distance between households was associated with reduced odds of linkage (OR: 0.46: 95% CI 0.44-0.48). Interpretation: Repeated introductions of measles virus from southwestern Utah seeded transmission elsewhere in Utah, with household, school, and sports exposures contributing to onward transmission. Validated genome-based linkage measures can complement contact tracing by helping public health teams identify likely transmission networks and prioritize investigation when resources are constrained.

after.abstract: Understanding the durability of vaccine-induced immunity is critical for evaluating long-term protection and vaccine scheduling, particularly in aging populations where immunosenescence may alter immune response dynamics. In this study, we used a novel mathematical modelling pipeline to quantify age-related differences in the contraction and persistence phases of gE-specific CD4+ T cell and anti-gE antibody responses following Shingrix vaccination. Specifically, we developed a semi-mechanistic model to expand virtual populations that captured inter-individual variability in peak concentrations and waning dynamics. To compare immune responses across age groups, we introduced a time varying, age-related immune advantage metric that measures the probability of a randomly selected younger individual exhibiting a stronger immune response than one from an older group. By evaluating this metric across multiple simulated virtual populations, our results demonstrate clear and sustained age-related differences in both gE-specific CD4+ T cells and anti-gE antibody responses, with younger age groups consistently exhibiting higher responses. Given these age-related differences, we used our model to explore alternative vaccine schedules in older age groups. These exploratory simulations suggest that booster doses administered between 6 and 12 months following the second dose may mitigate age-related differences in antibody dynamics. This work highlights the use of mechanistic mathematical modelling to disentangle age-associated differences in vaccine outcomes and lead to designing of plausible improvement in age-specific vaccine schedules.

after.abstract: Introduction: Elevated blood pressure variability (BPV) is predictive of Alzheimers disease neuropathologic change observed with AD biomarkers. However, prior studies have largely focused on visit-to-visit BPV, which may be influenced by antihypertensive medication adherence and other external factors. Few studies have investigated beat-to-beat BPV, a reliable and direct measure of cardiovascular and autonomic function relevant to AD. Methods: Independently living older adults (N=132) were recruited from the community. Participants underwent continuous blood pressure monitoring and venipuncture. Plasma p-Tau217, p-Tau181, GFAP, NfL, and amyloid-{beta}42/40 ratio were assessed. Linear regression examined the relationship between beat-to-beat systolic BPV and plasma AD biomarkers with and without adjustment for age, sex, systolic blood pressure, and apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) carrier status. Results: Elevated beat-to-beat BPV was associated with elevated plasma p-Tau217 ({beta}=0.32, p=0.008), plasma p-Tau181 ({beta}=0.22, p=0.05), and plasma GFAP ({beta}=0.41, p=0.00001). Elevated BPV was not associated with plasma amyloid-{beta}42/40 ratio or plasma NfL. Discussion: Increased beat-to-beat BPV is associated with increased Core 1 T1 biomarkers of phosphorylated and secreted AD tau in blood plasma (i.e., pTau217, pTau181), but not with amyloid-{beta}42/40 ratio, a biomarker more exclusively indexing cerebral amyloid retention alone. Elevated BPV was also associated with higher plasma GFAP, a marker of astrocyte reactivity. These findings are consistent with prior studies relating visit-to-visit BPV to AD biomarkers, suggesting that intrinsic cardiovascular and/or autonomic factors underlie links between BPV and AD.

after.abstract: Background: The increasing use of genetic testing has identified thousands of KCNH2 variants associated with long QT syndrome type 2 (LQT2), yet most remain variants of uncertain significance (VUS). Translating functional abnormalities into clinically actionable evidence remains a major challenge. We established a nationwide functional genomics strategy to systematically characterize KCNH2 variants identified in the French LQT2 population and improve their clinical interpretation. Methods: We characterized 303 KCNH2 variants, including 201 VUS, using standardized high-throughput automated patch-clamp electrophysiology and complementary membrane trafficking assays. Nine electrophysiological parameters were integrated using MeTAL to predict variant-specific repolarization phenotypes under homozygous and heterozygous conditions. Modeled QTc values were compared with patient electrocardiographic data and variant-specific penetrance estimates. Functional evidence was calibrated against established benign and pathogenic variants using ClinGen-recommended categorical OddsPath and continuous likelihood-ratio approaches. Results: Multidimensional functional profiling revealed abnormalities not captured by current amplitude alone, identifying additional variants with clinically relevant repolarization defects. Among variants assessed under heterozygous conditions, MeTAL predictions showed 82.9% concordance with patient QTc phenotypes for ACMG class 5 variants, with apparent discordances partly consistent with incomplete penetrance. Continuous likelihood-ratio calibration demonstrated strong discrimination between established benign and pathogenic variants (AUC=0.936) and provided graded functional evidence for 76.1% of VUS. Integration of calibrated functional evidence into the ACMG/AMP framework enabled reclassification of 64 of 201 VUS (31.8%), including 7 as pathogenic, 46 as likely pathogenic, and 11 as likely benign. Conclusions: This nationwide study establishes a scalable framework integrating high-throughput electrophysiology, computational modeling, and clinical phenotyping to translate complex KCNH2 channel dysfunction into clinically interpretable evidence. The resulting reclassification of nearly one-third of VUS, together with the open-access HAMMER database, provides a resource to improve molecular diagnosis and risk assessment in LQT2.

after.abstract: Background Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) myocarditis affects up to 2% of patients on ICI and has up to a 50% mortality. Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) is a risk factor for ICI myocarditis. Objectives: To leverage a multi-omics approach to evaluate cytokines associated with ICI myocarditis, immunosuppression resistance, CHIP in ICI myocarditis and implicated pathways and cell type contributions. Methods 236 cardio-oncology patients were enrolled, including 88 who were on ICI. Cytokine profiling from patients on ICI were sampled and analyzed using machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence. Single-cell multi-omics of peripheral blood from Yale (n=19), Stanford (n=25), and MGH (n=63) evaluated cell-type contributions of cytokines and implicated pathways. Validation of Yale proteomic analyses was done using the Stanford CYTOF dataset. Results Top features associated with ICI myocarditis included IL13, CXCL10, PDGFA, CCL13, CCL17 and KITlg. Top KEGG pathways associated with ICI myocarditis and immunosuppression resistant ICI myocarditis included JAK STAT signaling, IL17 signaling and lipid/atherosclerosis pathways. At the single-cell level, the consensus signals distinguishing myocarditis from non-myocarditis across cohorts was predominantly driven by module-level JAK STAT, T cell, and Toll like receptor activation. Similar transcription gene programs were activated in CHIP carriers including modules implicated in the pro-inflammatory immune response, such as NF kappa B, IL17, MAPK, and TNF pathways within CHIP cells spanning lymphoid (cytotoxic CD8+ NKT, and natural killer cells) and myeloid lineages. Conclusions Across cohorts, JAK STAT signaling emerges as a convergent and potentially actionable axis in ICI myocarditis that is further amplified in CHIP carriers, supporting cytokine-guided risk stratification and JAK STAT directed immunosuppression as testable strategies.

after.abstract: Artificial intelligence models for echocardiography interpret studies without identifying the structures that support their outputs. We show that this spatial grounding does not emerge from the pretraining of current vision-language models. General-purpose and medical vision-language models and an open-vocabulary detector recalled 3% or fewer of cardiac structures and scored below a box that never sees the image. EchoLens, a detector trained on 5,912 expert-annotated structures and 4,219 Doppler signals from 136 patients, recalled 87% and localized structures as reliably as a blinded expert reader (box centre within the reference in 95.7% and 95.3% of cases). It covers 21 structures across 11 transthoracic views and 11 spectral Doppler signal types. In external data, two physicians judged 81-92% of its detections correct across all 11 views, and it identified the Doppler signal type in 83% of frames. EchoLens provides the spatial layer that grounded echocardiographic interpretation requires.

after.abstract: This protocol describes the RED-WHF trial, a randomized, active-controlled, two-period crossover clinical trial designed to evaluate whether Sacred Dances (SD)--as a mind-body intervention--are non-inferior to conventional physical training (PT) regarding functional capacity and quality of life in women with heart failure (HF). Sedentary behavior and emotional stress significantly worsen HF prognosis, yet conventional exercise programs face barriers in patient adherence and variable motivation. Sacred Dances, a form of low-to-moderate-intensity moving meditation, may enhance physical fitness while promoting emotional well-being and spiritual connection (flourishing). We will recruit 30 sedentary women aged 18 to 70 with stable HF (NYHA class I-III) and a documented left ventricular ejection fraction. Participants will be randomized 1:1 to one of two treatment sequences: SD followed by PT, or vice versa. Each 12-week intervention phase consists of two weekly sessions, lasting 90 minutes for SD (with 60 minutes of active dancing to allow choreography instruction) and 60 minutes for PT, separated by a 3-week washout period. Primary outcomes are functional capacity (6-minute walk test [6MWT]) and health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L Index and VAS). Secondary outcomes include adherence rates, spiritual attitudes (ARES scale), symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress (DASS-21), and perceived subjective impact (EUPI-12). Statistical planning incorporates linear mixed models (LMM) with treatment, period, and sequence fixed effects, and an intention-to-treat approach with multiple imputation for missing data. To establish non-inferiority, a 30-meter margin for the 6MWT difference will be applied. The study was approved by the local Ethics Committee (CEP/EBMSP opinion 7.443.180, CAAE: 86133125.0.0000.5544) and prospectively registered in the Brazilian Registry of Clinical Trials (ReBEC ID: RBR-85tkdz5).

after.title: Preprint: Discrete dynamic survival analysis of epidemic case line lists
after.authors: Montes-Olivas, S.; Abbott, S.; Funk, S.; Gravenor, M. B.; Frost, S. D. W.
after.author_corresponding_institution: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
after.abstract: Case line lists, which record dates of onset, recovery, and hospitalisation, are among the most granular data in infectious disease epidemiology and can provide insights into transmission dynamics. Dynamic survival analysis (DSA) fits a deterministic, differential-equation-based model to line lists to estimate parameters such as infectivity and the infectious period. Infectious periods are usually not exponential, and incorporating this into mechanistic models for line-list data often requires partial differential equation (PDE) schemes that can be difficult to implement and must be customised for each model, which may limit their use. Here, we propose Discrete Dynamic Survival Analysis (DDSA), a discrete-time DSA for case line lists based on difference equations. It matches calendar-day data directly without interpolation, and its log-likelihood is differentiable via forward-mode automatic differentiation, enabling off-the-shelf gradient-based samplers without model-specific numerical infrastructure. Non-exponential infectious periods are accommodated through a boxcar model or a discrete analogue of the "device of stages". We apply the DDSA method to three historical outbreaks of influenza A(H1N1), Ebola, and measles. DDSA estimates of transmission parameters were close to published analyses where these were available, an agreement that partly reflects shared modelling choices, and the method handles incomplete line lists with missing onset or recovery dates. Synthetic experiments show that recovery intervals identify the infectious period, while infection times and final size constrain R0 when the population at risk is known. Discrete DSA provides a simple, extensible framework for simulation and inference of infectious disease dynamics.

after.abstract: Background Atrophic gastritis (AG), characterized by chronic inflammation of the gastric mucosa and glandular atrophy, is an established precursor of gastric cancer (GC) and contributes to iron-deficiency anemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, and pernicious anemia. Although Helicobacter pylori infection is a major environmental determinant, not all infected individuals develop AG or GC, suggesting that host genetic factors influence susceptibility to AG and severe atrophic gastritis (SAG). Previous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of AG have been limited in size and have not adequately compared anti-H. pylori IgG serostatus strata, leaving potential genetic heterogeneity unresolved. Methods We performed GWAS meta-analyses of AG and SAG, stratified by anti-H. pylori IgG serostatus, involving 214,747 Japanese participants: 75,074 in the discovery phase and 139,673 in the replication phase. Subsequent analyses included genotype-by-serostatus interactions, HLA allele and ABO blood group associations, genome-wide genetic correlations, multi-trait analysis, local genetic correlations, and structural equation modeling. In addition, cross-ancestry meta-analyses were performed using chronic gastritis GWAS data from FinnGen, UK Biobank, and the Million Veteran Program, comprising 1,357,053 participants. Results Across six Japanese GWAS meta-analyses, we identified genome-wide significant associations at 17 genomic regions. Strong associations with seropositive AG/SAG were observed at previously reported GC susceptibility loci, including PSCA and MUC1/MTX1, whereas the MHC class II region showed predominant associations with seronegative AG/SAG. FAP, CCR6, and ATP4A were also found to be associated with seronegative SAG. The identified regions included previously reported GC susceptibility regions MUC1/MTX1, PRKAA1/PTGER4, PSCA, ABO, and MHC. Associations at PSCA and MUC1/MTX1 were replicated at a genome-wide significance level, supporting a shared genetic basis between AG/SAG and GC. Additional AG-associated candidate regions included BMP2, CCDC80, LRRC34, CPEB4, PGC/FRS3, and LMTK2, implicating epithelial regulation, immune responses, transcriptional regulation, and differentiation. A positive genotype-by-serostatus interaction for SAG was observed at MUC1/MTX1. HLA class II alleles, including HLA-DRB1*15:01 and HLA-DQB1*06:02, showed associations with seronegative AG/SAG. The LDSC genetic correlation between AG and GC was 0.529, and the MTAG estimated Omega correlation was 0.694. Local genetic correlation analysis and structural equation modeling further supported shared genetic components. Cross-ancestry integration of seronegative SAG with external chronic gastritis GWAS data identified an additional association at TPTEP1. Conclusions Our findings characterize the genetic heterogeneity of serologically defined AG/SAG according to anti-H. pylori IgG serostatus. They highlight epithelial and mucus barrier-related pathways in seropositive AG/SAG and immune-related pathways in seronegative cases, while also providing evidence of a shared genetic basis between AG and GC. Together, these results clarify the genetic basis of a GC precursor and are consistent with a continuum from chronic inflammation through atrophy to carcinogenesis. These insights may inform prevention strategies and personalized management of the diverse health consequences of AG.

after.title: Preprint: Prevalence of protective hepatitis B surface antibody levels and associated factors among women admitted for delivery at Kawempe National Referral Hospital, Uganda: A cross-sectional study
after.authors: KEMBABAZI, E.; OCAN, M.; IBANDA, H.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Makerere University CHS: Makerere University College of Health Sciences
after.abstract: Mother-to-child transmission sustains the burden of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in sub-Saharan Africa, yet little is known about whether women giving birth in Uganda are protected. We estimated the prevalence of protective hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) levels, described serological profiles and identified associated factors among women admitted for delivery at Kawempe National Referral Hospital, Kampala. In this cross-sectional study, 418 women were selected by systematic random sampling in 2024 and interviewed about socio-demographic characteristics, hepatitis B testing, vaccination and exposures. Anti-HBs was quantified by electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (protective: [≥]10 mIU/mL); other HBV markers were screened with a rapid test. Prevalence ratios were estimated with modified Poisson regression. Overall, 264 women (63.2%) reported vaccination: 203 during the current pregnancy and 61 before it only. Protective levels were found in 322 women (77.0%; 95% confidence interval [CI] 72.8-80.8): 50.6% of never-vaccinated women, 82.0% of those vaccinated before the current pregnancy only and 95.6% of those vaccinated during it. After adjustment, vaccination before the current pregnancy only (adjusted prevalence ratio 1.54; 95% CI 1.24-1.89) and during it (1.86; 95% CI 1.57-2.20) were associated with protection; no socio-demographic or behavioural factor was. Eighty-two women (19.6%) had no serological evidence of immunity or infection; 65 had never been vaccinated. Of 300 women who reported a previous negative test, 50 (16.7%) had never been vaccinated, and 68 of 250 vaccinated women with known completion status (27.2%) had not completed three doses, mostly because they were not told to return or forgot. The rapid test detected hepatitis B surface antigen in 21 women (5.0%), but discordant marker patterns suggest some false positives. One in five women reached delivery susceptible to HBV, largely because a negative test was not followed by vaccination. Linking every negative antenatal test to vaccination could close much of this gap.

after.title: Preprint: Delayed first contact in a universally insured population: time to care and COVID-19 outcomes in Mexican primary care
after.authors: GODINEZ VAZQUEZ, V. J.; Nieves-Ruiz, E. R.; Razo Mendoza, L. F.
after.abstract: Time from symptom onset to first care may be a modifiable determinant of COVID-19 outcomes, but it is rarely quantified in primary care. This retrospective cohort study included all 5,248 confirmed SARS-CoV-2 cases (RT-PCR or certified rapid antigen test) notified to the national surveillance system (SINOLAVE) by a large family medicine unit of the Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) in Leon, Mexico, between April 2020 and April 2021. Pandemic waves were classified using the official IMSS definition. Wave profiles were compared with chi-square tests and Bonferroni correction, and predictors of death were assessed by multivariable logistic regression, with sensitivity analyses adjusting for severity signs at first contact. Of the cases, 53.8% were female, mean age was 41.1 years, and 317 deaths (6.0%) were registered. Median time to first care was 3 days (interquartile range: 2-5). Case fatality was 3.0% among patients presenting within 3 days and 9.1% among those presenting later. Later presentation (> 3 days) was associated with death (adjusted odds ratio = 1.98; 95% confidence interval: 1.47-2.65), but the association was attenuated after adjustment for severity signs at first contact (adjusted odds ratio = 1.20; 95% confidence interval: 0.85-1.69), which were more frequent among later presenters (21.8% vs. 9.3%). From the first to the second wave, fever (76.1% to 56.9%), diabetes (22.8% to 9.6%), and case fatality (10.5% to 4.8%) decreased, whereas anosmia and dysgeusia increased (all p < 0.001). Surveillance data cannot distinguish clinical progression during delay from late presentation of already severe patients. Delay persisted despite universal entitlement to care, indicating that insurance coverage alone did not ensure timely presentation; prospective cohorts measuring severity at onset are needed.

after.title: Preprint: Investigating Indirect Genetic Effects on Neurodevelopmental Traits Across Development and Reporters: Triangulating Twin-comparison and Trio-PGS Approaches
after.authors: Chi, Z.; Kawakami, K.; Plomin, R.; McAdams, T.
after.abstract: Polygenic associations with neurodevelopmental traits may reflect both direct and indirect genetic effects. However, evidence separating these effects is limited and mixed, and rarely spans development or reporters, or triangulates across methods. We triangulated twin-comparison and trio-based analyses in the Twins Early Development Study, using eight polygenic scores (PGS) and repeated parent, teacher and self-reports of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) traits from ages 4 to 26. Analyses included up to 7,259 offspring with observed or imputed parental genetic data. Both approaches consistently supported direct genetic effects of ADHD and ASD PGS on corresponding traits, whereas evidence for within-trait indirect effects was limited. Cross-trait indirect effects emerged for several PGS, particularly in parent reports, and some were unexpectedly negative. These findings suggest that within-trait polygenic prediction of ADHD and ASD traits mainly reflects direct rather than indirect genetic effects, whereas cross-trait associations reflect some indirect genetic effects.

after.title: Preprint: How Does Psilocybin Affect Daily Life Experience and Behavior? Protocol For a Multimethod Ambulatory Assessment Study Within a Clinical Trial of Psilocybin for Depression
after.authors: Sutu, A.; Kaplan, D.; Raison, C. L.; Sauder, C. J.; Arconada Alvarez, S. J.; Pozzo, N. S.; Salako, Z.; Chen, Z. J.; Palitsky, R.
after.abstract: Introduction: Although psilocybin has shown promise for treating depression, responses vary considerably, with some individuals experiencing limiting improvement and even adverse effects. Research has largely relied on assessments conducted at discrete time points, providing limited insight into how post-psilocybin change unfolds in everyday life. The Dial-In study aims to characterize daily-life processes associated with differential responses to psilocybin, including factors associated with improvement or worsening following challenging dosing experiences. Methods and Analysis: Dial-In is a prospective, observational, multi-method longitudinal study embedded within a clinical trial administering 25 mg of psilocybin to up to 141 adults with major depressive disorder. Ambulatory assessments combine ecological momentary assessment (EMA) and voice diaries for 14 days pre- and post- dosing, and passive audio sampling via the Electronically Activated Recorder (EAR) for three four-day periods to characterize everyday affect, behavior, reflections, and social interactions. Outcomes include depressive symptoms, psychological well-being, and psychedelic-related adverse effects assessed through eight weeks post-dose. Analyses will examine whether affective sudden gains and losses, social support, interpersonal conflict, conversational focus, reflection and rigidity predict differential outcomes. Additional analyses will test whether these factors moderate associations between challenging dosing experiences and clinical outcomes. Ethics and Dissemination: The project was approved by WCG Institutional Review Board, with Emory University relying on WCG as the reviewing board. All participants provide written informed consent. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and scientific presentations.

after.title: Preprint: Generative AI Versus Primary Care Physicians from Plan Initiation to Long-Term Maintenance of Chronic Disease Self-Management: A Vignette-Based Validation Study
after.authors: Zhao, Z.; Yang, H.; Wang, Q.; Wang, Y.; Cheng, W.; Ma, X.
after.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may provide personalised and dynamically adjustable support for chronic disease self-management. However, previous studies have largely focused on isolated questions and a limited range of evaluation dimensions. Objective To compare the quality of self-management advice generated by GenAI and primary care physicians (PCPs) across multiple stages of chronic disease management and evaluation dimensions. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional, source-blinded comparative evaluation using 15 standardised vignettes of diabetes and hypertension derived from authentic primary care follow-up records. Each vignette comprised three sequential management stages, with medical accuracy, readability, and behaviour-change potential assessed across the three simulated stages; individualisation and multidisciplinary integration at plan initiation; contextual adaptability during acute adjustment; and empathy during long-term maintenance. The GenAI system and 22 PCPs independently generated advice which was independently rated by three cliniciansone each from general practice, endocrinology, and cardiology. across seven dimensions. Linear mixed-effects models were used for the primary comparisons, and case-level paired and physician-distribution analyses were conducted as robustness analyses. Results The GenAI system achieved estimated marginal means above 4.0 in all dimensions except readability. It scored significantly higher than PCPs in six of the seven dimensions, with adjusted mean differences ranging from 1.16 to 1.56 points (P<.001). Readability was the only exception, with no significant difference between GenAI and PCPs (-0.22, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.11; P=.19). The GenAI mean exceeded the individual means of all recruited PCPs in the six dimensions but ranked at approximately the 23rd percentile for readability. Conclusions Our findings indicated the GenAI system may generate more highly rated self-management advice than PCPs across most evaluated dimensions but offered no advantage in readability. These findings provide pre-implementation evidence for GenAI as a potential source of structured and adaptive chronic disease self-management support. Patient-level pilot studies and subsequent randomised trials are needed to determine its acceptability and effects on behaviour and clinical outcomes.

after.authors: Yum, Y.; Hwang, Y.-h.; Choi, W.; Raynaud, V.; Lynch, J.; Lee, J.-S.
after.abstract: Objective: This study aimed to project introduction timing and pathways of cholera conjugate vaccine (CCV) and combined typhoid-cholera conjugate vaccines (TCV/CCVs) in 39 low- and middle-income countries and to assess potential barriers to their routine immunization integration. Methods: Accelerated failure time models were fitted using oral cholera vaccine (OCV) introduction as a proxy for CCV adoption. Country-level estimates were standardized using observed post-WHO-prequalification introduction intervals for analogous vaccine transitions. TCV/CCV introduction timing and pathways were projected by combining standardized CCV estimates with a TCV introduction priority index based on typhoid burden and previous vaccination experience. Potential barriers to routine immunization integration were assessed using semi-quantitative scoring approach. Results: Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance (Gavi) eligibility, greater previous OCV experience, and higher cholera intensity were associated with earlier introduction times. After standardization, the median projected time to CCV introduction was 6.9 years after WHO prequalification, with 12 countries introducing within five years. The TCV/CCV projections comprised three pathways: CCV introduction followed by transition to TCV/CCV, direct TCV/CCV introduction and continued CCV use without TCV/CCV introduction during the analysis period. Projected introduction timing was not consistently aligned with routine integration barrier levels for either vaccine. Conclusions: These scenario-based projections provide an early indication of where and when demand may emerge and which countries may require additional programmatic or financing support. The findings can inform demand forecasting, market assessment, manufacturing and supply planning, investment decisions, and introduction preparedness, but the projections should be recalibrated as product-specific evidence becomes available.

TCV/CCV introduction timing and pathways were projected by combining standardized CCV estimates with a TCV introduction priority index based on typhoid burden and previous vaccination experience. After standardization, the median projected time to CCV introduction was 6.9 years after WHO prequalification, with 12 countries introducing within five years. The TCV/CCV projections comprised three pathways: CCV introduction followed by transition to TCV/CCV, direct TCV/CCV introduction and continued CCV use without TCV/CCV introduction during the analysis period. Projected introduction timing was not consistently aligned with routine integration barrier levels for either vaccine. Conclusions: These scenario-based projections provide an early indication of where and when demand may emerge and which countries may require additional programmatic or financing support. The findings can inform demand forecasting, market assessment, manufacturing and supply planning, investment decisions, and introduction preparedness, but the projections should be recalibrated as product-specific evidence becomes available.

after.authors: Azar, R. M.; Shang, Y.; Waters, E. L.; Mendonca, R. J.; Johnson, A.; Diefenbach, P.; Cacchione, P. Z.; Johnson, M. J.
after.abstract: Purpose: Robot-assisted therapy predominantly targets motor impairment, although post-stroke motor and cognitive impairments co-occur. We report user experience in a longitudinal deployment of a Rehab Community-based Affordable Robot Exercise System (RehabCARES) for delivering personalized motor/cognitive training. Methods: Six adults with chronic stroke (FM-UE 20-61; MoCA 22-28) completed 12 therapy visits with THEAbot, a reconfigurable 1-DoF robot. Rehab CARES also included a haptic/biometric dynamic difficulty adjustment controller and eight games characterized by cognitive processes and motor/cognitive demand. We report gaming preference, usage, and user experience (pain, exertion, usability, affect, workload) across therapy. Results: User experience varied, but generally, self-reported pain was low, perceived exertion was light to moderate, enjoyment was strong and stable, and sense of control increased while excitement plateaued. Workload showed decreasing frustration and effort. Game selection during therapy was partially consistent with motor/cognitive clinical profiles; preferences and perceptual abilities may have influenced choices. Usability scores exceeded acceptability at all time points, peaking at the final visit (86 +/- 4.5 out of 100). Conclusions: RehabCARES provided personalized motor/cognitive training to a heterogeneous cohort in a community-based setting, delivering a positive user experience. Hardware reconfigurability and motor/cognitive game variety likely enabled this success.

after.title: Preprint: Cross-cohort validation of EEG biomarkers using a pre-registered three-criterion framework: a demonstration in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
after.authors: Gebregergis, B. T.; Yhdego, H. G.; Teklu, T.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Pharmacy, College of Health Sciences and Comprehensive Specialized Hospital, Axum University, Axum, Ethiopia
after.abstract: Background. Despite decades of EEG biomarker development for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), no candidate has progressed to clinical deployment, partly because cross-cohort validation is rare. We aimed to develop and demonstrate a pre-registered three-criterion screening framework to identify which candidate EEG features show the combined properties required for biomarker translation: cross-sectional discrimination, within-subject reliability, and cross-cohort effect consistency. Methods. We pre-registered a validation framework adapted from FDA-NIH BEST principles and applied it to 18 EEG features across three independent cohorts: EEGET-ALS (six ALS patients, 170 healthy controls; home recordings over 17 days), UCL/Penn State (eight ALS patients; clinic recordings over 1-2 months), and a healthy adult test-retest reference (60 participants, three sessions over one month). Features were required to meet three pre-registered criteria: (1) cross-sectional discrimination (Cohen's d > 0.5), (2) within-subject reliability (ICC(3,1) > 0.6 in both ALS cohorts independently), and (3) cross-cohort effect direction consistency. Cross-cohort permutation testing (1000 iterations) and subject-level bootstrap resampling (500 iterations) were applied to assess robustness. Results. Three features met all three pre-registered criteria: gamma power, theta power, and spectral entropy. Cross-cohort permutation testing showed that no permutation, out of 1000, produced any feature in the three-cohort reliability intersection (Monte Carlo p = 0.001). Bootstrap resampling indicated that the composition of the selected set was sensitive to sample composition (median count 1, 95% CI [0, 4]), with gamma power (67% inclusion), spectral entropy (43%), and theta power (32%) the most stable features at a relaxed reliability threshold (ICC > 0.5); at the primary pre-registered threshold (ICC > 0.6), the corresponding inclusion probabilities are lower (57%, 27%, and 19%, respectively). A principal methodological finding was that cross-cohort differences in feature reliability were large relative to the apparent disease-associated signal, most clearly demonstrated by relative beta power (ICC = 0.09 in a home-recorded cohort versus 0.93 in a clinic-recorded cohort); because recording protocol, hardware, setting, population, and preprocessing all differ jointly between cohorts in this dataset, this is evidence of cohort-associated variability that plausibly includes a protocol contribution, not a separately identified, isolated protocol effect. Conclusions. This study provides a pre-registered, multi-cohort EEG biomarker screening framework for ALS with explicit bootstrap-quantified uncertainty. Gamma power, spectral entropy, and theta power are identified as priority candidates for prospective validation. A recurring methodological observation is that protocol-related cohort differences appear to contribute more to cross-cohort variability than disease-related effects within this dataset; because protocol is confounded with cohort, equipment, and preprocessing, this pattern is descriptive rather than causal. The observation nonetheless has direct implications for the design of multi-site EEG biomarker studies in neural engineering.

after.abstract: Neuroinflammation is increasingly recognised as a key contributor to frontotemporal dementia (FTD) pathophysiology, yet how inflammatory processes relate to neurodegeneration and clinical progression remains poorly defined. This study aimed to identify a multivariate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) inflammatory signature covarying with brain atrophy, and to determine its relevance to clinical and cognitive outcomes in genetic FTD. We recruited 234 participants (non-carrier controls n=78, presymptomatic carriers n=115, symptomatic carriers n=41) with CSF, MRI, and clinical (CDR (r) + NACC FTLD sum of boxes [CDR-SB]) and executive (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Revised Digit Symbol Substitution Task [DSST] assessments. A regularised canonical correlation analysis (rCCA) was used to derive a shared protein-brain covariance axis. Participants were followed annually for up to 8.6 years (CDR-SB) and 11.5 years (DSST), and linear mixed-effects models were used to estimate individual rates of clinical progression (CDR slope) and executive decline (DSST slope). The predictive value of the inflammation- and MRI-based profiles for cross-sectional CDR-SB, CDR slope, DSST and DSST slope were tested in linear models. Due to floor effects and violations of parametric assumptions, Bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) confidence intervals (CI) and bootstrap CIs (95%, 5000 replicates) were utilised as the primary inferential criterion in the 2nd-level linear models; effects were considered non-significant if the 95% BCa CI crossed zero. The rCCA identified a robust inflammation-brain axis (r=0.89, p<0.001), driven by CXCL9, FLT3L, CCL3, and frontotemporal-insular atrophy pattern. In symptomatic carriers, the MRI canonical variate was associated with CDR-SB (beta=3.80, CI: [0.64, 6.20]) at baseline, whereas the inflammatory protein canonical variate was predictive of CDR-SB slope (beta=0.24, CI: [0.02, 0.46]). Whereas both MRI (beta= -7.27, CI:[-14.20, -1.00]) and protein (beta= -7.83, CI:[-14.00, -2.16]) canonical variates were linked to DSST cross-sectionally, but not longitudinally. No significant associations were found in pre-symptomatic carriers or non-carrier controls. A data-driven CSF inflammatory signature, covarying with frontotemporal-insular atrophy, tracks with clinical severity and cognitive impairment in people with genetic FTD, highlighting inflammation as a candidate therapeutic target and progression biomarker in the earliest clinically manifest stages of disease.

after.authors: Moreda, B. S.; Alem, S. G.; Worku, W. Y.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Addis Continental Institute of Public Health
after.abstract: Background Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of preventable blindness. Because it is asymptomatic until substantial damage has occurred, periodic retinal examination is essential for early detection. Evidence on uptake where eye services are co-located with diabetes care in Ethiopia is lacking. This study assessed the prevalence of, and factors associated with, adequate diabetic retinopathy screening practice among adults with diabetes attending Menelik II Comprehensive Specialized Hospital, Addis Ababa. Methods We conducted an institution-based cross-sectional study from December 2023 to February 2024 among adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes on follow-up for at least three months, selected by systematic random sampling and interviewed with a structured questionnaire. Knowledge and attitude were classified using a modified Bloom's cut-off of 80%, and screening practice as adequate when at least two of three recommended practices were met. Factors associated with adequate practice were identified using multivariable logistic regression. Results Of 404 patients approached, 371 were interviewed and included in the analysis (response rate 91.8%). Adequate screening practice was found in 139 participants (37.5%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 32.7-42.5); 62.0% had adequate knowledge and 72.8% a favorable attitude. Adequate practice was associated with adequate knowledge (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 5.10, 95% CI 2.81-9.25), a known eye disorder (AOR 3.96, 95% CI 2.11-7.43), higher education (AOR 3.82, 95% CI 1.33-10.95), age 41-65 years (AOR 3.15, 95% CI 1.10-9.03) and being married (AOR 1.73, 95% CI 1.01-2.97). Cost, lack of time and travel distance were the most commonly reported barriers. Conclusion Fewer than four in ten adults with diabetes underwent retinal examination at the recommended frequency despite on-site specialist eye care. The strong association with existing eye disorders suggests that examination is often prompted by ocular problems rather than undertaken for prevention. Strengthening patient education during diabetes follow-up and a direct referral pathway to on-site eye services may improve uptake.

after.abstract: Although cognitive decline and dementia are common at advanced ages, a fraction of individuals reach extreme ages maintaining high levels of cognitive function. Here, we compared whole-exome sequencing data from 136 cognitive superagers, individuals whose memory performance matches normative expectations for persons ~30 years younger, to 114 average-cognition controls and the gnomAD population reference database. While standard single-variant and burden analyses did not identify exome-wide significant loci, a rare variant allele frequency analysis identified 114 significant rare coding variants enriched in cognitive superagers. We highlight ten significant missense variants in genes implicating neurovascular biology (LOX, CLEC4M, CBWD6), immune regulation (HLA-B, HLA-DRB1, ITGAX, MUC4, MUC1), and neuronal structural (CEP131 x2). Together, these findings support an extreme-phenotype strategy as a tractable discovery framework for rare coding variation and nominate a set of biologically plausible loci to reveal potential genetic mechanisms for resilience to age-related cognitive impairment.

after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Basic Health Sciences, Universidad Rey Juan Carlos, Alcorcon, Spain
after.abstract: Background: EMFRA is a brief scale developed to assess physical, cognitive, emotional, and social functioning in older adults. This study examined its initial psychometric properties. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted with 201 older adults aged [≥]65 years without a diagnosis of dementia, recruited from the community, day-care and nursing centres from Madrid. Dimensional structure was examined through bootstrap parallel analysis (PA), bootstrap exploratory graph analysis (EGA), and factor analysis (FA), followed by progressive item refinement. Internal consistency, test-retest reliability in a subsample (n = 22), SEM, MDC95, floor and ceiling effects, and associations with SPPB, MoCA, Barthel Index, and HADS were assessed. Results: The 21-item version did not reproduce the four hypothesized domains, yielding a three-dimensional solution with limited stability. A nine-item version comprised two factors, Autonomy and Psychological Distress, although FA fit was limited (TLI = 0.80; RMSEA = 0.13). A low hierarchical omega (0.409) did not support a total score, whereas factor reliability was adequate (omega = 0.840 and 0.785). Test-retest ICCs were 0.82 and 0.78, with wide 95% CIs. No floor or ceiling effects were observed. Autonomy correlated with SPPB (r = 0.751), MoCA (r = 0.697), and Barthel (r = 0.56), and Psychological Distress with HADS (r = 0.625). Conclusions: The nine-item EMFRA shows preliminary evidence of a two-factor structure whose factors should be scored separately. Its temporal reliability and measurement error remain uncertain, and external validation is required before clinical implementation.

after.abstract: Objective: To develop and evaluate AToP (Attribution to Temporal Patterns), a post-hoc explainability framework that converts per-token Integrated Gradients (IG) from a Transformer into structured temporal pattern narratives. Materials and Methods: AToP was applied to a single-stream Transformer trained on MIMIC-IV v3.1 (218,196 patients; 12.6% unplanned 30-day readmission). It mines frequent episodes from salient-token subsequences in the training cohort, aggregates attribution among patients whose records contain each token or pattern, and collapses near-duplicates by patient overlap. Validation used masking, reversed-order analysis, token-level faithfulness tests, and KernelSHAP comparison. Results: The Transformer achieved AUROC 0.77 and PR-AUC 0.34. Population-weighted attribution emphasized high-prevalence codes with small per-patient impact. Carrier-conditional attribution, the mean among patients with the token, surfaced rare high-attribution psychiatric markers including psychosis, self-harm overdose, suicidal ideation (SI), and severe major depressive disorder (MDD). Pattern-level attribution identified within-visit co-occurrences and cross-visit trajectories not captured by token rankings. Risk-increasing patterns included psychiatric sequences ({MDD, SI} [->] SI) and oncologic progressions (cancer anemia [->] ascites). Obstetric and chest pain evaluation patterns were associated with lower predicted readmission. Discussion: The framework provides two complementary views of model predictions: carrier-conditional aggregation highlights rare, highly attributed clinical features, while temporal pattern analysis identifies within-visit combinations and cross-visit trajectories missed by token-level rankings. Masking and visit-order reversal provided evidence of correspondence with model behavior, but pattern attributions do not represent unique effects or establish clinical validity. Conclusion: AToP turns a Transformer's attributions into visit-anchored temporal pattern narratives, showing which events, in which order, contribute to its readmission predictions.

after.title: Preprint: Beyond one-off training: Continuing support, system stability and worker-borne costs shape electronic community health reporting in Kisii County, Kenya
after.authors: Adoyo, M. A.; Koringo, E. B.
after.abstract: Kenya's electronic community health information system (eCHIS) moves household and service data from community health promoters' phones into the national health information system. When reporting quality falls short, the usual response is more training and competency frameworks. We tested whether user capability and one-off training explain how well the system performs for its users, or whether continuing support and system stability matter more. We also examined where along the reporting chain quality was lost. In this convergent mixed-methods cross-sectional study in Kisii County, we surveyed 343 eCHIS users in 22 facility catchments, observed five sites against a structured checklist, and interviewed 13 key informants. Hierarchical ordinal and logistic regression with facility-clustered standard errors modelled user satisfaction and perceived system consistency. Formal eCHIS training was near universal (94.5%) and was not associated with either outcome. Adding continuing support (refresher training, mentorship and technical support response time) significantly improved both models. McFadden's pseudo-R{superscript 2} for consistency rose from 0.06 to 0.16. Each faster level of technical support response almost doubled the odds of reporting a consistent system (adjusted odds ratio 1.87, 95% CI 1.35-2.58). Each step up in crash frequency reduced the odds of higher satisfaction (0.60, 0.43-0.84). Digital comfort remained independently associated with both outcomes. At the observation sites, form logic secured completeness (all required fields were filled at 5 of 5 sites), but timeliness (2 of 5), consistency over time (1 of 5) and use of reports for decisions (0 of 4) failed, mostly because of synchronisation. In open-ended responses, 43.4% of respondents raised the cost of data bundles. Informants described promoters paying for connectivity and reinstalling the failing application themselves. Reporting quality depended less on what users knew than on the support around them. Competency frameworks will need matching standards for connectivity financing, support response and synchronisation monitoring.

after.title: Preprint: Readiness Among Female Community Health Volunteers to Deliver Community Based Tobacco Cessation Counseling in Rural Nepal: A Two-phase Mixed-methods Study
after.authors: Jha, O.; Chaulagain, B.; Bhusal, S.; Thapa, A.; Sharma, S.; Gautam, P.; Seals, A.; Pantha, A.; Bhattarai, M.; Acharya, B.; Pokharel, Y.
after.abstract: Tobacco cessation support is largely absent from health facilities in Nepal, particularly in rural areas. Female community health volunteers(FCHVs) serve communities across the country and could help extend cessation services, but it was unknown whether they can deliver tobacco cessation counseling. We evaluated their readiness to do so. Guided by the Health Belief Model, we conducted a two-phase mixed-methods evaluation with 28 volunteers in rural mid-Western Nepal. We held eight focus group discussions exploring the volunteers knowledge, confidence, and barriers to providing counseling, in two phases, eleven months apart. After the first phase we delivered a tobacco cessation training using lectures and role play, followed by a refresher training after the second phase, and we administered surveys before and after each training. We analyzed the qualitative data with deductive and inductive coding to identify themes, analyzed the surveys with descriptive statistics and Fishers exact test, and integrated the two sources to assess convergence and complementarity. The volunteers mean age was 48 years, one third had secondary education, and three quarters had served as volunteers for more than ten years. We identified five themes. In the first phase, volunteers had good knowledge of tobacco, its health effects, and cessation measures, recognized a role for themselves in counseling, and asked for regular training. In the second phase, their knowledge and confidence had improved, including trust that quitting is achievable, although some misconceptions and hesitation remained. They described personal, social, and policy-level barriers, such as community hesitation to engage in counseling, limited time, and easy access to tobacco products. Community receptivity to counseling improved over time, but the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted their efforts. Surveys showed that volunteers recognized their role and routinely provided counseling, while knowledge, confidence, and perceived barriers remained relatively stable across surveys; concerns about inadequate incentives and motivation rose from 25% to 57.1% between phases. The qualitative and survey findings converged and complemented each other, with the qualitative data providing depth and the surveys showing numerical trends. Female community health volunteers want to provide tobacco cessation counseling, showed good knowledge and confidence, and reported growing community receptivity, but they face several barriers. Qualitative findings suggest that training improved their knowledge and confidence. Policymakers should consider addressing system-level barriers, including training support and the availability of tobacco products, and integrating volunteers into cessation services. Before wider adoption, future studies should evaluate whether volunteer-led tobacco cessation counseling is clinically effective.

after.title: Preprint: Antifolate resistance markers and complexity of infection in children with sickle cell anaemia receiving malaria chemoprevention in Uganda: a molecular sub-study of the CHEMCHA randomised trial
after.authors: Nambatya, W.; Ocan, M.; Okek, E. J.; Ndeezi, G.; Kalibbala, D.; Katairo, T.; Bwanga, F.; Nkosi-Gondwe, T.; Kirikumwino, J.; Ssenkusu, J.; Tukwasibwe, S.; Opoka, R.; ter Kuile, F. O.; Phiri, K. S.; Idro, R.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Makerere University CHS: Makerere University College of Health Sciences
after.abstract: Background Sickle cell anaemia (SCA) is a major public health problem in Uganda. Monthly sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) remains the standard malaria chemoprevention regimen despite widespread antifolate resistance in East Africa. We assessed Pfdhfr and Pfdhps resistance mutations and the complexity of infection (COI) among children with SCA receiving malaria chemoprevention. Methods This prospective study of antifolate resistance was nested within the CHEMCHA randomised controlled trial comparing monthly SP with weekly dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DP) for malaria chemoprevention. Participants were children with SCA aged 6 months to 15 years and attending Jinja and Kitgum hospitals in Uganda. Dried blood spots were collected at enrolment, study closeout, and during febrile episodes. Parasite DNA from microscopy-confirmed clinical malaria samples was genotyped by amplicon sequencing for Pfdhfr (N51I, C59R, S108N, and I164L) and Pfdhps (A437G, K540E, A581G, A613S, and A613T). COI was estimated using MOIRE. Results Complete Pfdhfr/Pfdhps haplotypes were resolved for 7-28 isolates per site and time point, and COI was estimated for 67 samples. The quintuple mutant (Pfdhfr IRN/Pfdhps GE) accounted for 85.7-100% of isolates across sites and time points; A613S and A613T were not detected. Pfdhfr I164L was detected in 2/9 isolates in Jinja at baseline and 1/8 at endline. The Pfdhps A581G mutant allele was absent at baseline (0/44 isolates) but was found in 1/8 isolates in Jinja and 3/34 in Kitgum at endline, including quintuple-plus-581G (sextuple) haplotypes in 1/8 and 2/27 isolates, respectively. Most infections were monoclonal (51/67, 76.1%). Conclusions The high prevalence of quintuple antifolate-resistant haplotypes and the detection of higher-level resistance markers, including emerging sextuple mutants carrying Pfdhfr I164L and Pfdhps A581G, call into question the continued use of SP for chemoprevention in children with SCA in Uganda and support evaluation of alternative regimens.

after.authors: Wakoli, D. M.; Rotich, B.; Mbugua, E.; Van Hulle, S.; Kipkoech, J.; Abel, L.; Katairo, T.; Kimachas, E.; Wesolowski, A.; Conrad, M.; Menya, D.; OMeara, W. P.
after.abstract: Seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) is an important malaria prevention strategy used widely in areas of West Africa with highly seasonal transmission. Monthly administration of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine (SPAQ) to young children during the high-transmission season substantially reduces malaria morbidity and mortality. SMC has recently been introduced in northern Kenya, where pastoralist communities experience intense malaria transmission. However, implementation in this setting presents unique challenges, including population mobility, vast distances, dispersed settlements, and high levels of parasite resistance to SP in parts of the region. Effective surveillance is needed to identify gaps in SMC delivery and uptake and to monitor threats to program effectiveness. We implemented an innovative sentinel-site surveillance approach in which every malaria case among SMC-eligible children at selected health facilities was investigated to identify gaps in SMC delivery, uptake, and effectiveness. We also assessed the prevalence of parasite alleles associated with SP and AQ resistance and examined their relationship with SMC uptake. Household travel was substantially more common than caregiver refusal among reported reasons for missing an SMC cycle. More than one-third of children presenting with malaria had missed their most recent SMC cycle, while 15% were within a few days of receiving the next scheduled cycle. The prevalence of SP resistance mutations was considerably lower than reported in other parts of East Africa: only 13.4% of infections carried the quintuple mutant haplotype IRNI/GEAA (PfDHFR 51I, 59R, 108N, PfDHPS 437G, 540E) associated with high level resistance to SP. However, the prevalence of resistance-associated mutations was higher among children who had recently received SMC. The allele associated with reduced susceptibility to AQ was not detected. Sentinel surveillance identified geographic and implementation gaps in real time, allowing program managers to target SMC distribution and community sensitization. Although the prevalence of resistance-associated mutations that could threaten SPAQ effectiveness was low, evidence of intrahost selection among children who had received SMC suggests that continued molecular surveillance will be important as SMC is scaled up in northern Kenya. This sentinel surveillance approach provides a practical framework for monitoring SMC implementation in remote, highly mobile populations while simultaneously tracking emerging threats to SPAQ effectiveness.

after.title: Preprint: Admission Rate, Indications, Maternal Outcomes, and Factors Associated with Mortality Among Obstetric Intensive Care Unit Admissions at a Tertiary Referral Hospital in Tanzania.
after.authors: SAMWEL, R.; Barabona, G.; Kimwela, H.; Samji, S.; Meza, W.; Abeid, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Aga Khan Hospital Dar es Salaam
after.abstract: Background About 0.07% to 8% of parturients will require intensive care unit (ICU) admission during pregnancy, childbirth or puerperium, with great regional variations. When this occurs, it increases morbidity, mortality, long-term physical and psychological sequelae as well as cost. This study sought to examine a five-year admission rate, indications and outcomes of parturients with severe morbidities admitted in the ICU at a tertiary referral facility and teaching hospital in Tanzania. Methodology A retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted at Muhimbili National Hospital in Dar es Salaam city that included all women who were admitted to the obstetric ICU between 2019 and 2023. Data were retrospectively collected using a pre-tested checklist from all 1526 obstetric ICU admissions, out of 29391 obstetric unit admissions, during the study period. Sources of data were both case files and electronic registries in the ICU and labour ward. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with maternal mortality, with results presented as adjusted odds ratios (aOR) while indications of ICU admission and maternal outcomes were presented descriptively by using frequencies and tables. Results Out of 29391 obstetric unit admissions, 1526 required ICU, resulting into obstetric ICU admission rate of 5.2%. Hypertensive disorders were the leading cause of admission (73.7%) followed by obstetric haemorrhages (15%). Frequent ICU interventions included; mechanical ventilation (50%), anticonvulsants (26%), blood transfusion (15%), inotropes (4.2%), and dialysis (3.5%). Maternal fatality rate was 14%. In multivariable regression analysis, vaginal delivery was associated with 47% higher odds of mortality compared to caesarean section (aOR 1.47, 95% CI 1.03-2.11, p=0.036). A moderate ICU stay of 3-4 days showed a 91% protective effect relative to stays of [≤]2 days (aOR 0.09, P < 0.001). 5-7day stays were also protective (aOR 0.32, p=0.006). Anticonvulsant use was strongly protective against mortality (aOR 0.02, p < 0.001). Conclusion This five years review of obstetric ICU admissions (2019-2023) showed that, approximately one in 20 obstetric patients required critical care, with one in seven of ICU admissions resulting in maternal death. Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy accounted for majority of ICU admissions, and deaths occurred predominantly during the early phase of critical care. These findings underscore the need to strengthen antenatal risk identification, optimise referral and emergency obstetric care, ensure timely magnesium sulphate administration, and establish obstetric high dependency units to facilitate earlier interventions. Such measures could reduce the burden on ICUs while improving maternal outcomes.

after.abstract: Background: Over 3.5 million US men are living with prostate cancer (PCa). Certain per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are carcinogenic and impair cardiometabolic health. Due to comorbidities and treatment, men with PCa may be uniquely susceptible to PFAS. Objectives: To develop and validate a model for drinking water perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS), and perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA), and study associations of each PFAS with all-cause, PCa, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality in PCa survivors. Methods: We conducted a cohort study of 51,289 men with PCa diagnosed from 2006 to 2017 and followed through 2024 from the New Jersey (NJ) cancer registry. PFAS monitoring data (n=26,161 results) were obtained from NJ government evaluations and Community Water Systems (CWS) compliance reports and were used to estimate PFAS concentrations using a two-phase XGBoost model with 67 predictors of PFAS contamination across 566 CWS. PFAS predictions between 2006-2024 were linked to participant address histories. Adjusted hazard ratios (aHR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were estimated from Cox models with sociodemographic, clinical and time-varying neighborhood covariates. Results: There were 19,749 deaths, including 3,778 PCa deaths, and 4,972 CVD deaths over 466,843 person-years. Higher PFOA exposure was associated with all-cause mortality in certain quintiles (aHRQ2vsQ1: 1.07, 95% CI: 1.07-1.12; aHRQ3vsQ1: 1.06, 95% CI: 1.01-1.11) and with CVD mortality (aHRQ5vsQ1: 1.12, 95% CI: 1.01-1.24). Higher PFNA exposure was suggestively associated with all-cause mortality (aHR[≥]3.8ng/L vs <2ng/L: 1.22, 95% CI: 0.98-1.50) and PCa mortality (aHR[≥]3.8ng/L vs <2ng/L: 1.42, 95% CI: 0.96-2.10). Associations were strengthened when applying five-year lags. For example, higher PFOA (aHRQ5vsQ1: 1.15, 95% CI: 1.06-1.25), PFOS (aHRQ5vsQ1: 1.16, 95% CI: 1.07-1.25) and PFNA (aHR[≥]3.8ng/L vs <2ng/L: 1.57, 95% CI: 1.06-2.31) were associated with higher all-cause mortality. Discussion: Exposure to CWS-level PFAS was associated with higher mortality in PCa survivors. Replication is needed to confirm findings.
